text: I bought 7800XT for £420. It was Gigabyte OC version. It was obnoxiously loud under load, but reassuringly heavy. I had a few system freezes at the beginning,  but in general I was impressed. Then I tried Metro Exodus EE. When I turned up RT to max, my PC went to black screen and restarted. I tried many things. At the end I managed to keep it stable with undervolting and reducing power usage by 5%. Then I wanted to see how it would perform in 4K. Connected to my LG C1, and all hell broke loose. In 4K and high settings, no amount of tweaking would make it stable. Even Doom Eternal crashed it. So I connected it back to my 1440p monitor and surprise! It was still unusable. Any game or benchmark launch causes instant black screen and restart. The card is on it's way back to seller. Ordered 4070 super for £570. RX 7800XT would be a better value, if it only worked. Sadly. you can't put a price on peace of mind.

text:
Don't forget: this nVidia card should have been a "RTX 4080 12 GB Super" in the first place and should have sold for like 300 bucks more!

So for me, AMD strikes again. My favorite is not only the least expensive 7800 XT (or a used 6800 XT if you don't mind buying used) with less but more than capable performance for a noticeably lower price (and with more price adjustment coming in) but I have an eye on the 7900 XT and GRE models that in some cases also are targeting 600 € or below and are to be expected to settle on this mark quite soon.
Because with 20 Gigs of VRAM on the 7900 XT, similar or often better RT performance than 4070 Super and better rasterization performance it should become the new price/ performance king in the higher end!

I really don't like the limitations of nVidia with their few 12 Gigs of VRAM now. It reminds too much of that GTX 970 with 3.5 Gigs while RX 480 already came with 8 gigs. It's the same game over and over: for now 12 Gigs in 1440p are fine but there are already games using like 11.5 Gigs of it. So it's just a matter of time which is a win for AMD again, because many of their GPU age like fine wine.
And I do think gamers should not "reward" nVidia for pushing the midrange prices soo high. With more competition from AMD the pressure on nVidia would get higher which could result in better hardware for better pricing for us all.

I'm curious about why the RX 6800 XT (faster than the RX 7800 XT and RTX 4070 Ti) and RX 6800 (faster than the RTX 4070) perform so well in the Hogwarts Legacy 4K benchmark despite the RX 6700 XT performing so poorly in the same benchmark (slower than the RTX 4060 Ti).

If it's VRAM capacity, then the RTX 4060 Ti 16GB should be faster than the 8GB version and the 8GB version should be slower than the RX 6700 XT, and the RTX 3080 would not be able to perform so well.
If it's VRAM bandwidth, then the RX 6700 XT should be able to beat either version of the RTX 4060 Ti.
If it's GPU compute, then the RTX 4070 should be able to beat the RX 6800.

Does Hogwarts Legacy have some sort of inconsistent interaction between different aspects of the GPU design, an optimisation/driver bug on the RX 6700 XT, or a minimum GPU compute threshold (around 15TFLOPS) which needs to be reached in order to avoid being bottlenecked?

Radeon had the chance to take a HUGE chunk of the market after nvidia bait+switched their whole stack. All amd had to do was NOT do the same.  But they did. The $900 "7900XT" is what should have been a $650 7800XT, but radeon decided people wouldn't wake up after the crypto boom.
author: @forestR1

text:
RDNA3 was targeting a 70% uplift (like RDNA2 reached) but managed 36% at power parity (6950XT and 7900XTX are both 355W). From what insider gossip that has leaked we can gather that AMD thought they were fighting a driver bug right up until the boxes were printed and the AIBs were already putting components on cards... That's why the entire stack is completely mis-named. I own an XTX myself, but there is nothing that warrants that name. But calling it the 7800XT and giving it 24GB would have been weird, even if they had realized in time. AMD is ABSURDLY lucky that Nvidia went completely hamfisted on the prices this generation, or AMD would have had to tap out completely. The XTX is a 529mm2 die with an expensive packaging technology. If the 4080 had been $800 at launch AMD would have had to either fold, or sell at break-even, because a 378mm2 N4 chip on standard packaging is a lot cheaper to produce than a 304mm2 N5 chip + 6 38mm2 N6 chips on a new packaging technology.

It is what it is, and it's super unfortunate for pricing, but the observable raw numbers say that AMD fumbled. They didn't plan on this.

text:
@jaykay9975  The frame buffer is only one small component of VRAM, and on modern GPUs it can often entirely fit in the GPU's cache. The majority of VRAM is used to store texture and geometry data.
These terms have definitions, and misusing them only serves to mislead people. "Frame buffer" does not mean "VRAM capacity". They might sometimes be casually referred to as the same thing, like how some people use "graphics card" and "GPU" interchangeably, but they're not equivalent.

text: ​ @flipinfin  no, PSU of equal quality, just less powerful. You need to take into consideration the efficiency curve of the PSU as well, normally you'd want your PC to use around 60-80% of your PSU's capabilities, so it has some overhead when you need it and hits the efficiency curve both during high load and low load. Depending on the rest of the build of course, but for the most usual builds 1000W PSU would be an overkill for 4070S, you'd hit the efficiency range during full load, but at low load and idle you'd diminish energy efficiency advantage ever so slightly. Taking the HUB total system power draw figures of their test machine into consideration, to reach 60% of total PSU power you'd need a 600W PSU for a 4070S and 850W for a 6950XT, but since test figures are most likely a bit unrealistic, you'd want to throw in another 100-150W for other devices connected to the PC, so 750W for a 4070S and 1000W for 6950XT. So, let's consider a BeQuiet Straight Power 12 PSU series as our choice (the cheapest 80+ Platinum PSUs from a reputable manufacturer) that's $30-$60 price difference between 750W and 100W version depending on the deal, so already the advantage of 6950XT being $50 cheaper (not anymore) is almost completely gone.

author: @handyman1957

text:
@DarkOverFlowOverflow  I've helped a lot of people purchase and build computers or upgrades over the past almost three decades. This is my 99.5% sure-fire Radeon trouble shooting check list:

1) Reset BIOS to defaults, load XMP, set boot device and don't touch anything else. And if you must tinker, for the love of God, keep your mitts off the PCIe settings. And I highly recommend not tinkering until you've verified system stability over a several weeks long period.

2) If it's an upgrade from an Nvidia GPU: Clean reinstall of Windows. If the Windows install was previously on any other chipset than what this motherboard features: Clean reinstall of Windows.

3) Make sure the HDMI/DP cable is a proper name-brand one, and that it isn't any longer than it has to be. This one can seem strange, but Radeon is notoriously sensitive to cable quality. They have to be ON spec, not somewhat-close-to-spec.

I can't even begin to count the number of times this has magically resolved all AMD chipset/Radeon issues. There is something wonky with AMD (in general, also on the chipset side) and Windows' ACPI implementation. Steve even did a video on it a while back where he moved a Windows install from an Intel chipset to an AMD chipset and measured the (quite repeatable) performance drop. This seems to manifest itself for Radeon too. After many years I still haven't managed to track down the exact issue, but when you look in the event-log prior to a driver crash there is always an entry shortly prior from Windows ACPI engine. DDU does not fix ACPI tables. It just removes files and registry entries. For that reason I consider DDU a "within the same vendor only"-tool. It's great for fixing a crashed driver install/removal, or for rolling back a driver revision. But don't count on it as a cross-vendor cleanup tool.

The "USER ERROR DUH-HUH-HUH!!" approach of the other user is dumb as rocks. There is categorically no denying that AMD is still catching up, both in GPUs and chipsets, when it comes to system robustness. This makes it doubly important to run your system in the configuration that AMD will have spent the most time testing and verifying with: BIOS defaults and an "OEM spec" Windows install. If you don't attack the problem from this particular angle, that is in no way "user error". You tackle problems the way that has always worked for you, and AMD needs to work on robustness in non-standard situations.

I understand that you've returned your card now, but if any friends or family is in the same situation in the future, run them through the above check-list. And make sure they download the latest Windows ISO from Microsoft so it doesn't take three days of Windows Update to get a working system....

Have a nice day.

text:
@awebuser5914   that's not how this ever plays out. 
Consoles have the advantage of a fixed spec which allows for extremely efficient use of resources and 'tricks' that don't work when you're dealing with different hardware (colour palette tricks on the GBC & disc object location on X360/PS3 spring to mind, but I know of more modern equivilents).
PC's a) usually don't need to have their settings dialed back to hit a spec and b) usually get less efficient memory structures.
If the console has 16GB shared memory, your GPU needs ~16GB to match it... 
A 12GB card that can nearly match a console... for 20% more than the price of a console... is pathetic.

You're not wrong about 'bad PC ports' per say (we should have had texture download optimisations based on hardware years ago to reduce bloat), but looking at UE5 and the way the industry is going, I think you're being extremly naieve if you think things are going to get anything other than worse on that front.

TLDR 16GB is minimum 'gamer' spec now, and has been for 3½ years since AMD released the 6800XT... NV's just (intentially and maliciously) behind the curve.

text:
​@RafitoOoO Very true. Silicon prices for the latest process nodes have ballooned wildly with the increasingly expensive and difficult manufacturing processes. The 3nm fabs cost billions. It's something like $16,000 for a wafer of 3nm silicon from TSMC, which means that, if the max capacity of 90 potential chips all come out usable, which almost never happens, the chips cost a minimum of $177 USD each. The price only gets higher as you get defects. The upcoming 2nm process is slated to cost approximately 20k per wafer.
The manufacturing of silicon is absolutely brilliant, though. The lithography is a work of art fused with cutting edge technology to manufacture transistors that make a human blood cell look planetary. Incredible stuff, but expensive. If $200 is spent on the silicon alone, it's hard to imagine that upcoming GPUs with these newer processes will continue to be as affordable as they technically are.
author: @Malicious2013

text: ​ @sdtunstall That appears to be incorrect. Apparently, a wafer of 5nm GPU silicon runs around 17k, for a 300mm wafer. Assuming perfect yield, that's approximately 233 chips at just under $80 per 4070S chip... but reality is often disappointing, and there are often significant losses or defects. The actual yield is probably closer to 80%, give or take, if I had to guess. If they lose or downgrade 20% of the chips, each 4070S chip is closer to $100. That's before the cost of anything else, like heatsinks, PCB, and VRAM. All together, the production cost of the card might exceed $250-$300. Then, they estimate the expected volume sold and price accordingly to make whatever profit they can. That's more or less the jist of things.
